title: The I in Community: Social Trust for First-Year Students
abstract:
Reena Burt 

Faculty Advisor: Mesmin Destin

The I in Community: Social Trust for First-Year Students

Social trust plays a central role in our lives. According to the current literature, social trust is related to social and economic outcomes ranging from happiness and tolerance to civic engagement and societal economic growth to democratic functioning and decreased crime levels. Despite its importance, social trust has been declining in the U.S. since the 1980s. A trend driven by younger generations. Surprisingly, there is limited research on what impacts young adults’ social trust levels and why it is declining. To better understand the decline of social trust in younger generations, my study examines how specific identities, values, and character traits relate to young adults’ social trust. I conducted a mixed-methods study with 96 online survey responses and 9 semi-structured interviews from first-year students at a private mid-western university. Results showed that values of vertical collectivism (i.e. high family integrity and sociability with in-groups) are positively associated with trust in home communities whereas values of vertical individualism (i.e. competition and hedonism) are positively associated with trust in the university community. Identifying with more agent social identity groups was positively associated with social trust in the university community. These findings highlight two potential predictors of social trust that are understudied– individual and collective values and identity. This research has implications for institutions that seek to create a more trusting environment for all on college campuses.
